title: Episode 27: The Cricket War of 1848 and the Miracle of the Gulls
description:
In the spring of 1848, the pioneer settlers of Salt Lake City watched in horror as billions of flightless Mormon crickets swarmed from the foothills to devour their first green wheat crop. Facing certain winter starvation, the desperate settlers fought the black plague with fire, brooms, and ditches, until thousands of California gulls appeared in the sky, gorging on the insects and saving the settlement from destruction.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the summer of eighteen forty-seven, thousands of Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young completed an epic fifteen-hundred-mile exodus across the Great Plains and Rocky Mountains, arriving in the arid, sun-baked Salt Lake Valley. Exhausted and cut off from civilization, they planted nine hundred acres of spring wheat in eighteen forty-eight—their sole hope for surviving the coming winter. But in late May, just as the tender green shoots began to rise from the desert soil, an apocalyptic nightmare descended from the mountains: an army of billions of giant, flightless, flesh-eating insects that blackened the earth and devoured every living plant in their path. With starvation days away, salvation arrived from an unexpected quarter of the sky. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE PROMISED VALLEY AND THE GREEN SHOOTS
In July eighteen forty-seven, the vanguard company of one hundred and forty-three Mormon pioneers looked down from the mouth of Emigration Canyon onto the vast, shimmering expanse of the Great Salt Lake Valley. It was a harsh, unforgiving desert landscape dominated by sagebrush, greasewood, and blinding alkaline mud flats. Renowned mountain man Jim Bridger had famously warned the pioneers that nothing would ever grow in the arid basin, scoffing that he would gladly pay one thousand dollars for the first bushel of corn harvested from the valley soil. But Brigham Young, the resolute president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, looked out over the dry plain from his sickbed in Wilford Woodruff's carriage and declared: 'This is the right place.' Driven from Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois by years of bitter religious persecution, the pioneers sought a sanctuary so remote, arid, and isolated that no other settlers would contest it. That first winter was a grueling test of basic human survival; nearly two thousand pioneers lived in primitive adobe huts and canvas-covered wagon boxes, subsisting on thistle roots, wild sego lily bulbs, and boiled rawhide strips. As the spring sun of eighteen forty-eight warmed the valley floor, the settlers threw themselves into an agricultural miracle. Diverting icy mountain streams from City Creek and Red Butte Canyon into hand-dug irrigation furrows, they plowed and seeded over nine hundred acres of winter wheat, corn, and garden vegetables. By mid-May, magnificent carpets of tender emerald-green wheat shoots rose six inches above the dark earth, promising an abundant harvest that would feed the thousands of new pioneer families currently crossing the plains.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BLACK ARMY DESCENDS
In the final days of May eighteen forty-eight, an ominous, low humming sound echoed from the northern foothills of the Wasatch Range. Coming down the mountain canyons was an unimaginable ecological horror: billions of massive, flightless, armor-plated insects known to science as Anabrus simplex, and forever remembered as the Mormon cricket. Not true crickets, but giant, predatory shield-backed katydids measuring up to three inches in length, the creatures were glossy obsidian black, mottled reddish-brown, and terrifying to behold. Equipped with powerful, razor-sharp serrated mandibles capable of drawing human blood, the insects produced a sickening, ceaseless clicking sound that pioneers likened to the roar of a distant brushfire. They moved across the valley floor in a dense, writhing black carpet miles wide and up to six inches deep, devouring everything organic in their path—even chewing on the wooden handles of farming tools and the raw leather of settlers' work boots. As the black horde reached the tender irrigated fields, the destruction was swift and catastrophic. Millions of crickets swarmed up the wheat stalks, stripping every green leaf, tender node, and swelling grain head down to the dry soil within minutes. Where the swarm passed, vibrant green fields were transformed into blackened, barren waste smelling of insect excrement. Even more terrifying was the creatures' voracious cannibalism: whenever a cricket was trampled, dozens of its brethren swarmed violently over the crushed carcass, devouring it in seconds before surging on to consume the remaining wheat.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE DESPERATE BATTLE IN THE FIELDS
Faced with the certain prospect of mass starvation in the coming winter, the entire population of the settlement mobilized for total war. Men, women, and small children abandoned their homes and rushed into the fields with brooms, wooden paddles, and tree branches, frantically beating the ground in an exhausting attempt to crush the insects. Pioneers dug miles of deep ditches around their wheat fields, filling them with water to drown the hordes, but the crickets were so numerous that millions crawled over the floating bodies of their drowned comrades, creating writhing living bridges that allowed the horde to cross unhindered. Settlers hauled dry sagebrush and wheat straw into the fields, setting massive walls of fire to incinerate the swarms, but the blackened army marched directly into the flames, smothering the fires with their charred bodies by sheer numbers. Children beat tin pans and blew horns to frighten the pests away, but the crickets were utterly deaf and indifferent to noise. For two grueling weeks, the settlers fought eighteen-hour days under the blistering desert sun, their clothes soaked in sweat and cricket gore, their hands blistered, weeping openly as field after field of vital food disappeared into the black maw of the swarm.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BREAKING POINT AND THE FAST ON THE FRONTIER
By the first week of June, physical exhaustion and psychological despair had pushed the pioneer community to the brink of collapse. More than half of the tender wheat crop had already been wiped out, and the black insect carpet continued to pour unceasingly from the northern canyons, showing no sign of diminishing. In pioneer journals, mothers wrote heartbreaking entries expressing dread over how they would feed their infants when winter snows sealed the mountain passes. The colony was fifteen hundred miles away from the nearest supply depots in the Missouri Valley; if this first crop failed, no wagon train could possibly arrive in time to save them from mass starvation. Realizing that human strength and frontier ingenuity had failed, Brigham Young and the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles called a solemn assembly. On Sunday, June fourth, eighteen forty-eight, work in the fields ceased. The pioneers gathered in the central bowery of the infant city for a day of communal fasting and fervent prayer, pleading for deliverance from an ecological disaster beyond their mortal control. They acknowledged that without a miracle, their bold dream of a desert Zion would perish in the sand before it had even begun.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE WINGED CLOUD FROM THE GREAT SALT LAKE
On the afternoon of June ninth, eighteen forty-eight, five days after the solemn fast, a weary pioneer looked up toward the shimmering waters of the Great Salt Lake to the west and shouted in alarm. Rising from the islands of the inland sea was a colossal white cloud, sweeping eastward toward the valley like a gathering snowstorm. As the cloud drew closer, the settlers realized with dread that it was a massive flock of thousands of large, white birds: California gulls. At first, panic swept through the farming families; fearing that the birds had come to devour whatever sparse wheat was left in the fields, farmers ran through the furrows waving their arms and shouting to scare them off. But when the great flock settled across the blackened fields, the settlers witnessed an astonishing spectacle: the gulls ignored the grain entirely and began devouring the crickets with insatiable fury.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE FEAST OF THE GULLS
The voracity of the gulls surpassed anything the pioneers had ever witnessed. Flying low over the furrows, the white birds snatched up the giant black insects by the dozens, gulping them down whole until their crops were bulging. Then, in a behavior natural to nesting gulls feeding their young, the birds flew to nearby irrigation ditches, drank deeply of the fresh water, regurgitated great piles of half-digested crickets in small mounds along the ditch banks, and immediately returned to the fields to gorge themselves again. For days, the relentless air-to-ground assault continued. Thousands of gulls wheeled through the sky from dawn to dusk, diving into the swarms and consuming millions of crickets every single hour. Pioneer women and children watched in awe and relief as the black tide began to recede from the surviving wheat fields. By the time the gulls finished their feast and returned to their rookeries on Antelope and Egg islands, the vast cricket army had been completely broken. While hundreds of acres had been destroyed, enough of the winter wheat crop had been saved to sustain the pioneers through the winter, providing precious seed grain for the triumphant harvests of future years.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SACRED BIRD OF UTAH
The salvation of the eighteen forty-eight harvest became known throughout Utah history as the 'Miracle of the Gulls.' It forged a deep, enduring cultural bond between the people of Utah and the California gull. In nineteen thirteen, the Church erected a magnificent bronze monument on Temple Square in Salt Lake City: the Seagull Monument, designed by Brigham Young's grandson, sculptor Mahonri Young. Featuring two bronze gulls atop a towering granite column flanked by bronze relief plaques depicting the desperate battle, it is the only monument in the United States dedicated to honoring a bird. In nineteen fifty-five, the Utah State Legislature went even further, officially designating the California gull as the state bird of Utah and enacting strict legal penalties for anyone who harmed the creature. Today, when visitors to Salt Lake City see gulls wheeling gracefully over the desert valley hundreds of miles from the Pacific Ocean, they are reminded of the summer when an army of black crickets nearly starved a territory, and the winged miracle that descended from the clouds to save a civilization.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Cricket War of 1848 is an inspiring story of human resilience, ecological balance, and hope in the face of despair. It proves that in the grand tapestry of nature, salvation often comes on the wings of the unexpected. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we journey into the silver depths of Nevada and the miracle of the Sutro Tunnel. Until then, stay curious.
